item.title: AI-generated support, worked examples, and script-based learning in undergraduate physics: A comparative study
item.description: arXiv:2611.28951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support students during learning and problem solving, but its instructional value depends on how it is embedded in established learning approaches. Worked examples guide learners through the steps and reasoning of a solution; conversational AI may extend them by responding to individual questions. To isolate this added value, we compared a chatbot-delivered intelligent worked example with a matched static worked example and a lecture script. Nine recitation groups in an undergraduate electrodynamics course were cluster-randomized to the three conditions, and 86 students worked individually on a Gauss's law problem. Concept-test accuracy and self-efficacy increased significantly in all conditions, but changes did not differ significantly between groups (p=.07 for concept-test accuracy and p=.38 for self-efficacy). Four weeks later, in a reduced sample with selective participation and pre-existing group differences, students in the static worked-example condition scored higher than those in the script condition (p=.004, d=1.22), whereas the two worked-example conditions did not differ significantly. Usability, but not perceived educational value, was higher for the intelligent worked example than for the script (p=.011, d=0.88). In a subsequent homework assignment on Ampere's law with free choice of learning material (N=46), 62-71% of students in each condition reported using only the static worked example, at most 8% used exclusively the intelligent one, and 15-31% used neither. Thus, conversational delivery showed no clear additional learning benefit under the present conditions. More broadly, a learning format that is rated favorably need not be the one students voluntarily adopt.
item.dc:creator: Larissa Hahn, Marie Aylin Falkenberg, Marten Hogel\"ucht, Pascal Klein

item.title: Shaderous: A Browser-based Hydrodynamics Code for Physics Research and Teaching
item.description: arXiv:2611.31162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Shaderous is a three-dimensional code for compressible gas dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics that runs in WebGPU compute shaders in a web browser on any vendor's GPU. It combines an unsplit MUSCL-Hancock scheme and HLLC fluxes with a multigrid Poisson solver, block-structured adaptive mesh refinement with per-block timesteps, constrained transport with HLLD fluxes, point masses with sinks, gray radiation transport with the M1 closure, implicit pressure for low Mach numbers, tabulated equations of state from degenerate electrons to rock and iron, cooling, viscosity, conduction, resistivity, mixtures of gases, and nuclear burning by a neural network trained on a 13-isotope reaction network. A setup is shared as a link and runs on a student's own laptop or phone, so the code suits teaching at every level. A run is limited to one GPU: the largest adaptive mesh so far held about 175 million cells on an NVIDIA H200. It therefore suits parameter studies, run as sweeps from the command line, rather than the largest single simulations. Three aspects of the design are, as far as we can find, new. First, the hydrodynamic solver stores no face flux. The two cells that share a face compute bit-identical fluxes, so cells at boundaries between levels and between timesteps recompute their neighbors' fluxes instead of keeping a flux register. Mass, momentum and energy are conserved to round-off on the adaptive mesh, and compensated sums keep the divergence of the magnetic field at round-off. Second, the whole step runs on the GPU: the timestep and the assignment of blocks to time bins are reduced there, and ghost cells are computed as they are loaded rather than exchanged. Third, the code computes in single precision yet reproduces a range of astrophysical systems accurately, from stars and atmospheres in hydrostatic balance to shocks, gravitational collapse and magnetized flows, in 206 validation tests.
item.dc:creator: James Guillochon

item.title: Classical diamagnetism: How adiabatic change of field makes it work
item.description: arXiv:2606.20986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many textbooks discuss the diamagnetic response of a ``classical atom'' to a small and slowly (adiabatically) applied magnetic field. Here we show that the small-field assumption is not essential, whereas the slow rate of field change is crucial: it preserves the circular nature of the orbit regardless of the applied field magnitude. The latter property follows from the existence of an adiabatic invariant of electron's motion. Orbit circularity allows us to solve the problem for arbitrarily large fields. Resulting diamagnetic response exhibits symmetries that unexpectedly persist beyond the small-field limit, and provides a nice illustration of the range of applicability of Larmor's theorem.
item.dc:creator: Ya. B. Bazaliy, Ammar Kasem
